patches.name: Add
patches.summary: Adds numbers or vectors together, or joins pieces of text in order.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Add combines all of its inputs into one result, working from top to bottom.

- **Value 1, Value 2, …** are the values to add. Change the input count to add up to 32 values.
- Points, sizes, and other vectors add each component separately: [10, 20] + [5, 5] is [15, 25].
- Set the type to **Text** to join text instead. "Hello, " + "Sam" is "Hello, Sam". Numbers wired into a text Add turn into text.
- **Output** is the sum, or the joined text.

## Tips
- Space out looped layers: Multiply a Loop's Index by the row height, then Add a top margin.
- Order only matters for text. For numbers, 2 + 3 and 3 + 2 are the same.
- Keep a running total with a feedback wire: Output → Delay One Frame → back into Value 1.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **+** patch. Its unlabeled inputs are called Value 1, Value 2, and so on.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: The sum of all values, or the joined text when the type is Text.

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: A value to add, or a piece of text to join. Inputs combine from top to bottom.

commonMistakes: The label shows "12" instead of 3: the type is Text, so the numbers were joined. Set the type to Number to add them.
Words run together ("HelloSam"): text joins with no separator. Put the space inside one of the values, such as "Hello, ".

examples.title: Stack looped cards down the screen
examples.description: Each card sits 100 pt below the previous one, starting 120 pt from the top.

layer card rectangle "Card" @16,120 358x88 cornerRadius=16 position←place.output
patch rows loop count=5
patch spread multiply<point> value1←rows.index value2=[0,100]
patch place add<point> value1←spread.output value2=[16,120]

patches.name: Subtract
patches.summary: Subtracts one or more values from a starting value, such as finding how far apart two positions are.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Subtract starts with **Value 1** and takes away every input below it: Value 1 − Value 2 − Value 3 …

- **Value 1** is the starting value. Every other input is subtracted from it, in order.
- Points, sizes, and other vectors subtract each component separately: [100, 80] − [20, 30] is [80, 50].
- **Output** is what's left.

## Tips
- Find how far something moved: current position − start position, with the type set to Point.
- Flip a direction: 0 − value turns 40 into −40.
- Center a layer: screen width − layer width, then Divide by 2.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **−** patch. Its unlabeled inputs are called Value 1, Value 2, and so on.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index:
```
out = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) out = out - ctx.input(`value${i}`);   // left fold, component-wise
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: any result component that isn't finite (NaN or ±Infinity, e.g. from overflow past ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: − folds left from its base value. Import index and progress types as `number` and anchor as `point`.

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: Value 1 is the starting value; each later value is subtracted from the running result.

commonMistakes: The result has the wrong sign: inputs subtract from top to bottom, so Value 1 is the starting value. Swap the wires or reorder the ports.
A Point result moves on both axes: a plain number wired into a Point subtract becomes [n, n]. Build [n, 0] with a Point patch when you only want one axis.

patches.name: Multiply
patches.summary: Multiplies values together, for scaling a number, spacing looped layers, or turning 0–1 progress into distance.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Multiply starts with **Value 1** and multiplies it by every input below it: Value 1 × Value 2 × …

- Points, sizes, and other vectors multiply each component separately: [2, 3] × [10, 0] is [20, 0].
- A number wired into a vector Multiply scales every component by that number.
- **Output** is the product.

## Tips
- Turn 0–1 progress into points: progress × 300 moves something 300 pt.
- Reverse a direction with × −1.
- Space looped layers: Loop Index × 120 gives 0, 120, 240, …

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **×** patch. Its unlabeled inputs are called Value 1, Value 2, and so on.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index:
```
out = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) out = out * ctx.input(`value${i}`);   // left fold, component-wise
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0. There's no dot or cross product: [2, 3] × [4, 5] is [8, 15].
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: any result component that isn't finite (NaN or ±Infinity, e.g. from overflow past ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: × folds left. Import index and progress types as `number` and anchor as `point`.

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: A value to multiply by. Inputs combine from top to bottom.

commonMistakes: The output is stuck at 0: one input is 0, and anything times 0 is 0. Set multipliers you aren't using to 1, or lower the input count.
A slide goes the wrong way: positive values move right and down. Multiply by a negative number to move left or up.

patches.name: Divide
patches.summary: Divides a value by one or more values, outputting 0 with a warning instead of breaking when you divide by zero.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Divide starts with **Value 1** and divides it by every input below it: Value 1 ÷ Value 2 ÷ …

- Points, sizes, and other vectors divide each component separately: [300, 90] ÷ [3, 2] is [100, 45].
- Dividing by 0 outputs 0 for that component and shows a warning in the console, so layers don't vanish or fly off screen.
- **Output** is the result.

## Tips
- Normalize: scroll distance ÷ scrollable height gives 0–1 progress.
- Center a layer: (screen width − layer width) ÷ 2.
- Find a grid row: Loop Index ÷ columns, then Round's Rounded Down.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **÷** patch. Origami doesn't document what dividing by zero does; Sonobe outputs 0 and warns.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
out = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) {
  d = ctx.input(`value${i}`);
  out = d === 0 ? 0 : out / d;      // per component; warn once (below)
}
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Division by zero: when a divisor component is 0 (or -0), that component of the running result becomes 0 and later divisions keep it at 0. The patch warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`, naming the patch id and the port (for example `"divide_1: Value 2 is 0, so the output is 0."`). Other components still divide normally.
- Edge cases: any result component that isn't finite (NaN or ±Infinity, e.g. from overflow past ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: ÷ folds left. Its divide-by-zero result is undocumented (likely IEEE ±Infinity or NaN); imported files get 0 instead. Import index and progress types as `number` and anchor as `point`.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: Value 1 divided by every other value. Components divided by 0 output 0.

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: Value 1 is the value to divide; each later value divides the running result.

commonMistakes: The layer suddenly snaps to 0: a divisor reached 0, such as a size before layout or a Counter at 0. Keep the divisor at least 1 with Max, or check it with Greater Than first.
Scroll progress never reaches 1: dividing by the full content height ignores the part already on screen. Divide by content height minus screen height.

patches.name: Modulo
patches.summary: Outputs the remainder after dividing, for wrapping a count back to 0, finding grid columns, or alternating items.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Modulo divides **Value 1** by **Value 2** and keeps what's left over: 7 mod 3 is 1. As Value 1 counts up, the result climbs toward Value 2, then wraps back to 0 before reaching it, like a clock.

- Negative values wrap forward too: −1 mod 3 is 2, so a count going backwards still lands in range.
- Decimals work: 5.5 mod 2 is 1.5.
- Extra inputs apply again in order: (Value 1 mod Value 2) mod Value 3.
- Vectors wrap each component separately.
- Modulo by 0 outputs 0 and shows a warning in the console.

## Tips
- Grid column: Loop Index mod 3 gives 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2 …
- Every other row: Index mod 2 is 0 for even rows and 1 for odd rows.
- Keep an angle between 0 and 360: angle mod 360.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Mod** patch. For negative values Sonobe always wraps into the range between 0 and Value 2 (−1 mod 3 is 2). A code-style remainder, like JavaScript's `%`, gives −1; use Math Expression if you need that.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component (floored modulo):
```
r = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) {
  b = ctx.input(`value${i}`);
  if (b === 0) { r = 0; continue; }          // warn once (below)
  r = r - b * Math.floor(r / b);             // result has the sign of b
  if (Math.abs(r) >= Math.abs(b)) r = 0;     // round-off guard, e.g. -1e-17 mod 3
}
ctx.output("output", r === 0 ? 0 : r);       // normalize -0
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Sign: with `b > 0` the result is in `[0, b)`; with `b < 0` it's in `(b, 0]`. Examples: 7 mod 3 = 1, −1 mod 3 = 2, 7 mod −3 = −2, 5.5 mod 2 = 1.5.
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Modulo by zero: a divisor component of 0 sets that component to 0 and later steps keep it at 0. Warn once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`, naming the patch id and port.
- Edge cases: any result component that isn't finite (NaN or ±Infinity, e.g. from overflow past ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: Mod's sign convention is undocumented (its Math Expression % is JavaScript's truncated remainder). Sonobe uses floored modulo because wrapping is what designers use it for; results differ only when an operand is negative. Import index and progress types as `number` and anchor as `point`.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: The remainder, always between 0 and the divisor (0 included).

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: Value 1 is the value to wrap; each later value is a divisor applied to the running result.

commonMistakes: The last page never shows: mod 4 gives 0, 1, 2, 3, never 4. Use the number of items as Value 2, not the last index.
A result is almost Value 2 instead of 0: decimals aren't stored exactly, so 0.3 mod 0.1 comes out near 0.1. Work in whole numbers (3 mod 1) or Round first.

patches.name: Power
patches.summary: Raises a value to a power, for squaring numbers, doubling at each step, or bending 0–1 progress into a curve.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Power multiplies **Value 1** by itself **Value 2** times: 2 to the power 3 is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

- **Value 1** is the base and **Value 2** is the exponent. Extra inputs raise the result again, in order: (2³)² = 64.
- Exponents can be decimals or negative: 9 to the power 0.5 is 3, and 2 to the power −1 is 0.5.
- Vectors raise each component separately.
- Combinations with no real answer, such as a negative base with a decimal exponent, output 0 and show a warning.

## Tips
- Ease 0–1 progress: progress to the power 2 starts slow; to the power 0.5 starts fast.
- Zoom in doubling steps: 2 to the power of a level gives 1, 2, 4, 8.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Power** patch. Extra exponent ports chain from left to right.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
out = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) out = Math.pow(out, ctx.input(`value${i}`));   // left fold
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Math: `Math.pow` semantics. Any value to the power 0 is 1 (including 0⁰). A negative base with an integer exponent keeps its sign (−2³ = −8).
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: results with no real value (a negative base with a non-integer exponent, e.g. −8 to the power 1/3) and results that aren't finite (0 to a negative power, overflow) output 0 for that component. The patch warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: the docs describe "the base value to the subsequent exponents' powers", which we read as a left fold ((base^e1)^e2). Import index and progress types as `number` and anchor as `point`.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: The base raised to each exponent in turn.

variadic.name: Value
variadic.description: Value 1 is the base; each later value is an exponent applied to the running result.

commonMistakes: −8 to the power 1/3 gives 0 instead of −2: a negative base with a fractional exponent has no real answer here. Take Absolute Value, raise it, then Multiply by −1.
The curve bends the wrong way: exponents above 1 start slow and end fast. Use an exponent below 1, or the Curve patch, for a fast start.

patches.name: Square Root
patches.summary: Outputs the square root of a value, for undoing a square, sizing even grids, and working out distances.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Square Root finds the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the input: the square root of 9 is 3.

- **Value** is the number to take the root of. Vectors take the root of each component separately.
- Negative values have no real square root, so they output 0 and show a warning.
- **Output** is the root.

## Tips
- For the distance between two points, subtract them and use Length; it adds the squares for you.
- Lay out N items in a square-ish grid: the square root of N, rounded up, is the column count.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **√** patch.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
x = ctx.input("value");
ctx.output("output", x < 0 ? 0 : Math.sqrt(x));   // negative → 0, warn once
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Negative input: a component below 0 outputs 0 and the patch warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`, naming the patch id. `-0` outputs `0` without a warning.
- Edge cases: any result component that isn't finite (NaN or ±Infinity, e.g. from overflow past ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: √ documents its input as "a non-negative value" and doesn't say what negatives do; imported files get 0.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The value to take the square root of. Negative values output 0.

commonMistakes: The output stays at 0: the value going in is negative, like a position left of the origin. Take Absolute Value first, or use Length for distances.

patches.name: Absolute Value
patches.summary: Turns negative values into positive ones, for measuring how far something moved in either direction.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Absolute Value removes the minus sign: −40 becomes 40, 500 stays 500, and 0 stays 0.

- **Value** is the value to make positive. Vectors make each component positive separately: [−30, 40] becomes [30, 40].
- **Output** is the positive result.

## Tips
- Detect a swipe in either direction: Absolute Value of the drag distance, then Greater Than 80.
- Fade a card as it moves away from center either way: Absolute Value → Remap → Opacity.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Absolute Value** patch.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
x = Math.abs(ctx.input("value"));
ctx.output("output", x === 0 ? 0 : x);   // normalize -0
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: inputs are finite after coercion, so the output is always finite.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The value to make positive.

commonMistakes: A diagonal distance looks too small: Absolute Value works on each component separately, so [30, 40] stays [30, 40]. Use Length for the straight-line distance (50).

patches.name: Round
patches.summary: Rounds a number to the nearest whole number or decimal place, and also outputs it rounded down and rounded up.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Round cleans up long decimals. You get three results at once:

- **Rounded** is the nearest value. Halfway values round away from zero: 2.5 → 3 and −2.5 → −3.
- **Rounded Down** always goes toward the lower number: 2.7 → 2 and −2.3 → −3.
- **Rounded Up** always goes toward the higher number: 2.1 → 3 and −2.7 → −2.
- **Places** is how many digits to keep after the decimal point: with 1, 3.14159 becomes 3.1. Negative places round to tens (−1) or hundreds (−2).
- Set the type to Point or another vector to round each component, such as snapping a position to whole points.

## Tips
- Round outputs a number, so trailing zeros disappear (9.90 shows as 9.9). Use Format Number for display text with fixed decimals.
- Use Rounded Down to turn a Random value between 0 and 3 into 0, 1, or 2.
- To round to steps like 8 or 50, use Snap.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Round** patch, including the Places input added in version 195. Halfway values round away from zero.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component of `value`:
```
p = clamp(roundHalfAwayFromZero(ctx.input("places")), -15, 15);
k = 10 ** Math.abs(p);
n = p >= 0 ? x * k : x / k;
n = Number(n.toPrecision(15));        // strip binary noise: 1.005 × 100 → 100.5, 0.7 × 10 → 7
back = (r) => (p >= 0 ? r / k : r * k);
ctx.output("rounded",     back(Math.sign(n) * Math.floor(Math.abs(n) + 0.5)));   // half away from zero
ctx.output("roundedDown", back(Math.floor(n)));
ctx.output("roundedUp",   back(Math.ceil(n)));
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0. `places` is always a single number applied to every component.
- Precision: the `toPrecision(15)` step makes decimal inputs round the way they read. Golden values: (1.005, 2) → 1.01 / 1 / 1.01; (−2.5, 0) → −3 / −3 / −2; (0.7, 1) → 0.7 / 0.7 / 0.7; (1234.5, −2) → 1200 / 1200 / 1300; (−1.005, 2) → −1.01 / −1.01 / −1.
- Places: a non-integer places value rounds to the nearest integer first; values beyond ±15 clamp, since doubles hold about 15 significant digits.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: every output normalizes `-0` to `0` (−0.4 rounds to 0). Components with `|x| ≥ 2^53` are already whole and pass through unchanged. Inputs are finite after coercion, so no output is ever NaN or ±Infinity.
- Muted: the default bypass: all three outputs pass `value` through.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Round is number-only there; the vector variants are a Sonobe extension, and imported patches use `number`. Origami's handling of exact halves and negative places is undocumented. Sonobe rounds halves away from zero (like Foundation's default) and accepts negative places.

inputs.name: Places

outputs.description: Value rounded to the nearest step; halfway values round away from zero.

outputs.description: Value rounded toward the lower number (floor).

outputs.name: Rounded Up

A counter changes a step early: Rounded goes up at the halfway point. Use Rounded Down when a value should only change after passing each whole number.

patches.name: Min
patches.summary: Outputs the smallest of its inputs, for capping a value from above or picking the shorter of two sizes.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Min compares all of its inputs and outputs the smallest one.

- Use it as a ceiling: Min of a value and 300 follows the value but never goes above 300.
- Vectors compare each component separately: Min of [10, 50] and [30, 20] is [10, 20].
- Change the input count to compare up to 32 values.

## Tips
- Need a floor and a ceiling at once? Use Clamp.
- Size a card to the smaller of its content height and the screen height.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Min** patch. Its unlabeled inputs are called Value 1, Value 2, and so on.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
out = ctx.input("value1");
for (i = 2; i <= ctx.inputCount; i++) out = Math.min(out, ctx.input(`value${i}`));
ctx.output("output", out === 0 ? 0 : out);   // normalize -0
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0. Components compare independently, so the result can mix components from different inputs: min([10, 50], [30, 20]) is [10, 20].
- Input count: `ctx.inputCount` is 2–32 (default 2). Removing ports drops their values; added ports start at the variadic default.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: inputs are finite after coercion, so the minimum is always finite.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.
- Coming from Origami: Min's docs also mention color and index types. Index values arrive through the `number` variant; color isn't a variant here (compare channels with Color to RGB). Import position types as `point` and anchor as `point`.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: The smallest input, compared component by component for vectors.

commonMistakes: The value never drops below the number you typed: that's Max. Min caps from above, so Min of a value and 300 never goes over 300. Use Max for a floor, or Clamp for both.

patches.name: Max
patches.summary: Outputs the largest of its inputs, for keeping a value from dropping below a limit or picking the taller of two sizes.

- Vectors compare each component separately: Max of [10, 50] and [30, 20] is [30, 50].
- Change the input count to compare up to 32 values.

## Tips

- Keep a divisor from reaching 0: Max of the divisor and 1.

patches.name: Clamp
patches.summary: Keeps a value between a minimum and a maximum, so scrolling, dragging, or progress can't go past its limits.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Clamp lets a value through untouched while it's between **Min** and **Max**. Past either limit, the output holds at that limit.

- **Value** is what you want to keep in range.
- **Min** is the lowest allowed value and **Max** is the highest. If Min is greater than Max, Clamp swaps them, so the order doesn't matter.
- Vectors clamp each component separately, which keeps a point inside a rectangle.

## Tips
- Clamp progress to 0–1 before a Transition so a bouncy scroll can't push the animation past its ends.
- Bound a feedback loop: Add → Clamp → back into Add keeps a running total inside a range.
- Converting ranges anyway? Remap has a Clamp to Range option.

## Coming from Origami
This is Origami's **Clip** patch, renamed so it isn't confused with a layer's Clip Contents. Clip only handles numbers; Clamp also handles vectors. Origami doesn't document Min greater than Max; Clamp swaps them.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Each frame, for each loop index, per component:
```
a = ctx.input("min"); b = ctx.input("max");
lo = Math.min(a, b); hi = Math.max(a, b);          // min > max: limits swap
out = Math.min(Math.max(ctx.input("value"), lo), hi);
ctx.output("output", out === 0 ? 0 : out);
```

- Variants: `number` is a single component; `point` and `size` have 2 components, `point3d` 3, `point4d` 4. Vector variants apply the operation to each component independently. Coercion happens at connect time (ARCHITECTURE.md §4): a number wired into a vector variant broadcasts to every component, and a boolean arrives as 1 or 0. Swapping also happens per component.
- Equal limits: `min == max` outputs that number for every value (not an error).
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values. There's no history, so nothing is seeded.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: inputs are finite after coercion, so the output is always finite.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Clip's formula is `min(max(value, min), max)`, which returns Max when Min > Max. Sonobe swaps the limits instead; imported files differ only in that case. Clip is number-only, so imported patches use `number`.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The value to keep in range.

inputs.name: Min
inputs.description: The lowest value allowed through.

inputs.name: Max
inputs.description: The highest value allowed through. If it's below Min, the two limits swap.

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: Value, held between Min and Max.

commonMistakes: The layer won't move at all: Min and Max are equal (both 0 after changing the type), so every value holds at one number. Set Max to the far limit, such as the content height.
The layer still slides past the edge: Clamp only changes its own output. Wire Clamp's Output into the layer's Position, not the original value.

patches.name: Remap
patches.summary: Converts a value from one range to another, like turning scroll distance 0–150 into a header height from 120 to 64.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Remap answers "when the input is here, what should the output be?" Set the two ends of each range and everything in between follows along.

- **Value** is what you're reading, such as a scroll offset or a drag position.
- **From Start** and **From End** are the input range. **To Start** and **To End** are the outputs at those two points.
- Past the input range, the output keeps going beyond To Start and To End. Turn on **Clamp to Range** to hold it at the ends.
- Either range can run backwards (From Start 200, From End 0) to flip the direction.
- Set the type to Point, Size, or Color to map onto those: scroll 0–100 can fade a background from white to black.
- **Curve** (advanced) eases the values in between instead of changing at a steady rate.

## Tips
- Collapsing header: Value from the scroll offset, From 0 → 150, To 120 → 64, Clamp to Range on.
- If From Start equals From End, Remap acts like a switch: To End once Value reaches From Start, To Start below it.

## Coming from Origami
Remap does the job of a Progress patch feeding a Transition patch, in one patch.
patches.behavior:
Stateless, apart from a per-instance warned-once flag used by the edge-case warning below.

Each frame, for each loop index:
```
v = ctx.input("value"); a = ctx.input("fromStart"); b = ctx.input("fromEnd");
p = a === b ? (v >= a ? 1 : 0)             // zero-width range acts as a step (CONVENTIONS.md §18.5.9)
            : (v - a) / (b - a);           // unclamped
if (ctx.input("clampToRange")) p = Math.min(Math.max(p, 0), 1);
e = (p >= 0 && p <= 1) ? ease(ctx.input("curve"), p) : p;   // outside 0–1 the curve isn't applied
out = toStart + e * (toEnd - toStart);     // component-wise
ctx.output("output", out);
```

- Curve: `ease` is the Penner easing for the selected CURVE option (semantics.md §7.8); `linear` returns `p`. Every curve maps 0 → 0 and 1 → 1, so extrapolating with `e = p` outside 0–1 keeps the output continuous. A zero-width range gives `p` of exactly 0 or 1, so the curve doesn't change the step.
- Variants: `value`, `fromStart`, and `fromEnd` are always numbers; `toStart`, `toEnd`, and `output` follow the variant. Vectors interpolate each component. Colors interpolate in straight RGBA (gap-fill R12) and each channel clamps to 0–1 after interpolation; no other variant clamps unless Clamp to Range is on.
- Reversed ranges need no special case: the formula handles `fromEnd < fromStart` and `toEnd < toStart`, and Clamp to Range still holds the output between To Start and To End.
- Frame 0: evaluates with the authored values; there's no history.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index. The output length is the longest input loop; shorter loops wrap and scalars broadcast. An empty loop produces an empty output.
- Edge cases: any output component that isn't finite (for example, a huge Value over a tiny range overflowing ±1.8e308) outputs 0 for that component and warns once per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`. `-0` is output as `0`.
- Restart and dispose: restart clears the warned-once flag. Nothing to dispose.

inputs.description: The input value that produces To Start.

inputs.description: The input value that produces To End. It can be smaller than From Start.

inputs.name: To Start

inputs.name: To End

Nothing changes as you scroll: the input range doesn't match what Value actually does (scrolling down often makes the offset negative). Look at Value with a Watch patch, then set From Start and From End to the numbers you see.

patches.name: Snap
patches.summary: Moves a value to the nearest step or point, and can use flick velocity to predict where it lands, for grids and carousels.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Snap works like a magnet: it moves a value to the nearest allowed spot. Use it for grids, carousel pages, and places a card should settle.

- **Value** is the number or position to snap.
- **Mode** picks the spots. **Step** uses evenly spaced values: Offset, Offset + Step, Offset + 2 × Step, and so on. **Points** uses the closest value in the **Points** loop.
- **Velocity** (points per second) lets a flick carry the value further before it snaps, the way a flicked carousel lands on a later page. Leave it at 0 to snap to what's nearest right now.
- **Output** is the snapped value, and **Index** says which spot won: the step number, or the position in Points (−1 if Points is empty).
- With the type set to Point, Step snaps each axis separately (a step of 0 leaves that axis free), and Points picks the closest point in a straight line.

## Tips
- Snap only on release: use If / Else to pass the raw position while the finger is down and Snap's output after, then feed a Spring Animation.
- **Deceleration** (advanced) matches Scroll's momentum. Normal carries a flick about half a second of travel; Fast stops sooner.
- Keep the result in bounds with Clamp, such as between the first and last page.

inputs.name: Value
inputs.description: The number or position to snap.

inputs.name: Velocity
inputs.description: Flick speed in points per second, used to predict where Value lands before snapping. 0 snaps to the nearest spot now.

inputs.name: Mode

enumOptions.name: Step
enumOptions.description: Snap to evenly spaced values: Offset plus whole multiples of Step.

enumOptions.name: Points
enumOptions.description: Snap to the closest value in the Points loop.

inputs.description: Whether to snap to evenly spaced steps or to a list of points.

inputs.name: Step
inputs.description: Space between snap spots in Step mode, in points. 0 turns snapping off for that axis.

inputs.name: Offset
inputs.description: Where the first step sits in Step mode; spots are Offset + n × Step.

inputs.name: Points
inputs.description: The allowed spots in Points mode, as a loop.

inputs.name: Deceleration

enumOptions.name: Normal
enumOptions.description: Slows like a standard scroll fling (0.998 per millisecond).

enumOptions.name: Fast
enumOptions.description: Stops sooner, like a fast-decelerating scroll view (0.99 per millisecond).

inputs.description: How far Velocity carries the value before snapping, matching Scroll's momentum settings.

outputs.name: Index
outputs.description: Which spot was chosen: the step number from Offset (negative below it), or the position in Points, or −1 when Points is empty.

outputs.name: Projected
outputs.description: Where Value would land from its velocity, before snapping.

commonMistakes: The layer jumps between spots while you drag: Snap works every frame, not only on release. Pass the raw position while the finger is down (If / Else on Down) and the snapped position after.

A flick flies several pages past where you expect: Velocity is in points per second, so a per-frame difference or a scaled value projects too far. Wire the Velocity patch's output, or set Deceleration to Fast.
Points mode never snaps: the Points loop is empty, so Output passes the value through and Index is −1. Build the loop with Loop Builder.
